docs.title: Welcome to Wobsongo
docs.text: This documentation provides a comprehensive overview of Wobsongo, an open-source misinformation detection tool. It covers the core architecture, the document processing pipeline, and local development practices.

docs.title: Project Overview & Features
docs.text:
Wobsongo is an open-source backend engine for misinformation detection, powered by a knowledge management and hybrid retrieval system. It provides infrastructure to ingest content, build a structured knowledge base, and verify claims against it.

  • REST API: Written in Go using the Echo framework, providing a high-performance, low-latency API.
  • Async Job Queue: Powered by River on PostgreSQL for reliable processing of long-running background tasks.
  • Document Storage: PostgreSQL for structured data with S3-compatible object storage (MinIO locally) for documents and media assets.
  • Extensible Architecture: Clean layered design (handlers → services → repositories) with interface-based abstractions, making it straightforward to add new storage backends, job workers, or verification modules.

docs.title: SDG Alignment
docs.text:
This project contributes to:

  • SDG 3 (Good Health & Well-being): By providing infrastructure to combat health misinformation.
  • SDG 16 (Peace, Justice, Strong Institutions): By enabling transparent fact-checking of public information.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Jetify's Devbox (ensure it's installed on your system).

Devbox uses the Nix package manager under the hood to provide reproducible development environments.

By running devbox shell, it will automatically download and set up the required versions of the tools specified in the devbox.json file, such as:

  • Go
  • Node.js and pnpm
  • Make, PostgreSQL, Air, Swag, etc.

Note that subsequent commands assume you are inside the devbox shell.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
1. Clone the repository:

    git clone git@github.com:kairosedubf/wobsongo.git
cd wobsongo

  2. Activate Devbox environment:

    devbox shell

    You should see your shell prompt change, indicating you are now inside the devbox environment:

    (devbox) ➜  wobsongo git:(main) _

  3. Install backend dependencies (inside devbox shell):

    go mod download

    Optionally, run the linters:

    make check

    See Makefile for more details.

    You can run the unit tests with:

    make test-unit

    ...or the entire test suite with:

    make dbtestup test dbtestdown

docs.title: Running the Project
docs.text:
• Run the backend (with hot-reloading):
make dev
  • You should see the server running:
Starting the server at localhost:8000

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Wobsongo is structured around a strict layered architecture with one governing rule:

Every part of the system that needs to interact with data or trigger business logic uses the service layer.

Repos are private implementation details of services. HTTP handlers, background workers, and CLI commands never access repos directly — they call services.

docs.title: The Layers
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  HTTP Handlers  (handler/)              │
│  Workers        (worker/)               │  ← all callers go through service
│  CLI            (cmd/)                  │
├─────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Services       (service/)              │  ← single entry point for all logic
├─────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Repos          (repo/)                 │  ← private to services
├─────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  DB             (db/)                   │  ← SQLC-generated
└─────────────────────────────────────────┘

Cross-cutting:
  data/   → repo + external provider interfaces
  model/  → domain models
  queue/  → background job definitions

Dependencies flow downward only. No layer reaches upward.

docs.title: Handlers (handler/)
docs.text:
HTTP transport only.

  • Bind and validate the incoming request DTO.
  • Call one service method.
  • Write the response.

Handlers contain no business logic. If you find yourself doing an if on domain data in a handler, it belongs in the service.

docs.title: Services (service/)
docs.text:
All business logic lives here.

  • Services are the only layer that depends on repo interfaces (data/).
  • When multiple SQL operations must succeed or fail together, the service calls repo.WithTx() and composes individual atomic repo calls inside.
  • When an operation must atomically write to the DB and enqueue a background job (e.g., create a record and send a notification), both happen inside a single WithTx() call via txRepo.Enqueue().

docs.title: Repos (repo/)
docs.text:
Private to services. Not part of the public API of any package.

  • Each method performs exactly one SQL statement.
  • No repo method calls another repo method.
  • No repo method manages its own transaction.
  • Maps database types (SQLC output) to domain models (model/).
  • Maps database errors to typed application errors (e.g., ErrNotFound, ErrConflict).

docs.title: Workers (worker/)
docs.text: Workers implement river.Worker[T] and process background jobs. They call service methods, never repos or DB queries directly. A worker is just another caller of the service layer.

docs.title: CLI Commands (cmd/)
docs.text: Management commands (migrations, seed data, admin operations) use service methods for any data operations. No command handler should open its own database connection for business logic.

docs.title: Transactions
docs.text:
Transaction boundaries are owned by the service layer.

Correct:

// Service composes atomic repo methods in one transaction
func (s *DocumentService) Ingest(ctx context.Context, form *dto.IngestDocumentDTO) error {
    doc := buildDocument(form)
    return s.repo.WithTx(ctx, func(txRepo data.DocumentRepoer) error {
        if err := txRepo.Create(ctx, doc); err != nil {
            return err
        }
        // Job is enqueued in the same transaction — atomically
        return txRepo.Enqueue(ctx, &queue.ProcessDocumentDTO{ID: doc.ID})
    })
}

Incorrect:

// Repo manages its own transaction — NOT allowed
func (r *DocumentRepo) IngestAndEnqueue(ctx context.Context, ...) error {
    return pgx.BeginFunc(ctx, r.pool, func(tx pgx.Tx) error {
        // multiple SQL ops...
    })
}

The first version keeps all business decisions in the service. The second hides them in the data layer where they can't be tested without a database.

docs.title: Interfaces (data/)
docs.text:
The data package defines Go interfaces for every repo and external provider. Services depend on these interfaces, not on concrete implementations. This is what makes unit testing possible: mocks (in mockrepo/) implement the same interfaces.

Repo interfaces embed data.TxAware[T] when they need transaction support, and queue.JobEnqueuer when they need to enqueue jobs:

type DocumentRepoer interface {
    GetByID(ctx context.Context, id uuid.UUID) (*model.Document, error)
    Create(ctx context.Context, doc *model.Document) error
    // ...
    data.TxAware[DocumentRepoer]
    queue.JobEnqueuer
}

docs.title: Adding a New Feature
docs.text:
Follow this checklist top-down:

  1. Model — add or extend a struct in model/
  2. SQL — write the query in sql/queries/, run make gen to regenerate db/
  3. Repo interface — add the method to the relevant interface in data/
  4. Repo implementation — implement the method in repo/ (one SQL op per method)
  5. Mock — regenerate the mock via make gen
  6. Service — add the business method in service/, compose repo calls, handle transactions
  7. Handler — add the HTTP endpoint in handler/, call the service method
  8. Test — write service-level unit tests using the mock repo

docs.title: ADR 0001: Layered Architecture with Service-Layer Entry Point
docs.text: Status: Accepted Date: 2026-07-06

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Wobsongo is a Go backend. As the codebase grows, we need a clear, enforceable rule about what belongs where — otherwise business logic, transaction management, and database access tend to scatter across layers, making the system harder to test, understand, and maintain.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
We adopt a strict layered architecture with one primary rule:

Any part of the system that needs to interact with data or trigger business logic uses the service layer. The service layer is the single entry point for all business logic.

Repos are private implementation details of services. Handlers, workers, and CLI commands never touch repos directly.

docs.title: The Layers
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  HTTP Handlers  (handler/)              │  ← transport only
├─────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Services       (service/)              │  ← ALL business logic lives here
├─────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Repos          (repo/)                 │  ← private to services
├─────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  DB             (db/)                   │  ← SQLC-generated, never hand-edited
└─────────────────────────────────────────┘

Cross-cutting:
  data/   ← repo + provider interfaces (the contracts)
  model/  ← domain models
  queue/  ← job definitions and JobEnqueuer interface

docs.title: Rules per Layer
docs.text:
Handler (handler/) - Parse and validate the incoming request (DTO binding + go-playground/validator). - Call exactly one service method. - Format and write the response. - No business logic. No direct repo access. No transactions.

Service (service/) - Owns all business logic. - Is the only layer that depends on repo interfaces (data/). - Orchestrates transactions: when multiple SQL operations must be atomic, the service calls repo.WithTx(ctx, func(txRepo) error { ... }) and composes individual atomic repo calls inside. - Enqueues background jobs via repo.Enqueue(), optionally inside WithTx() for atomic write + enqueue.

Repo (repo/) - Implements interfaces defined in data/. - Each method performs exactly one SQL statement. No repo method calls another repo method. No repo method manages its own transaction. - Maps database errors to application-level errors (e.g., pgx.ErrNoRows → ErrNotFound). - Maps db.* types (SQLC output) to model.* types.

DB (db/) - SQLC-generated code from SQL files in sql/queries/. - Never edited by hand.

Workers (worker/) - Implement river.Worker[T]. - Call service methods for all business logic — never touch repos or DB directly.

CLI commands (cmd/) - Use service methods for any data operations — no direct DB connections in command handlers.

docs.title: Transaction Pattern
docs.text:
// ✅ Service composes atomic repo methods in a transaction
func (s *DocumentService) Ingest(ctx context.Context, form *dto.IngestDocumentDTO) error {
    return s.repo.WithTx(ctx, func(txRepo data.DocumentRepoer) error {
        if err := txRepo.Create(ctx, doc); err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if err := txRepo.Enqueue(ctx, &queue.ProcessDocumentDTO{ID: doc.ID}); err != nil {
            return err
        }
        return nil
    })
}

// ❌ Repo manages its own transaction — NOT allowed
func (r *DocumentRepo) IngestWithSetup(ctx context.Context, ...) error {
    return pgx.BeginFunc(ctx, r.pool, func(tx pgx.Tx) error {
        // multiple SQL ops...
    })
}

docs.title: Interface Composition for Atomic DB + Enqueue
docs.text:
When a repo needs to support both transactional DB operations and job enqueuing in the same transaction, its interface embeds both:

type DocumentRepoer interface {
    Crudable[model.Document]
    data.TxAware[DocumentRepoer]
    queue.JobEnqueuer
}

docs.title: Mock Convention
docs.text: Mocks are generated by moq and live in mockrepo/. Each interface in data/ should have a corresponding mock. Mocks are triggered by //go:generate directives in the interface source file.

docs.title: Anti-Patterns to Avoid
docs.text: Anti-pattern Why it's wrong Repo method calls pgx.BeginFunc or pool.Begin Transactions belong at the service layer Repo method does more than one SQL statement Breaks testability; obscures business logic Worker opens its own DB connection Bypasses service layer; breaks observability CLI command calls db.Queries directly Same as above Service imports db directly Services should depend on repo interfaces, not SQLC output

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Services become a readable, testable boundary: all business logic is visible in one place.
  • Each repo method is trivially mockable (one SQL op = one mock call).
  • The rule is verifiable in code review: does this repo method contain more than one q. call? Does this worker import repo?
  • New features follow a predictable checklist: model → SQL query → repo method → mock → service → handler.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text: /api/v1/* currently has no authentication applied. This is a known limitation of the current release, not an intentional "public by design" choice — if you're deploying this beyond a trusted internal network, put it behind your own auth layer (a gateway, a reverse proxy with API-key checking, a VPN, etc.) until first-class API authentication lands.

docs.title: What exists in the codebase but isn't wired up
docs.text: The codebase includes handler.PSKAuthMiddleware — a pre-shared-key checker that expects an Authorization: PSK <key> header and compares it in constant time — along with BOT_EXTRACT_PSK/BOT_CALLBACK_PSK environment variables. Neither is currently attached to any route. They exist as groundwork for a future bot-integration auth scheme, not as something you can rely on today. Don't set those env vars expecting them to protect anything yet.

docs.title: How the web UI differs
docs.text: The bundled web UI (/login, /dashboard, /documents, etc.) is authenticated separately — via a JWT stored in an HTTP-only cookie plus CSRF token validation on state-changing requests. That scheme is scoped to the HTML routes and doesn't extend to /api/v1/*. See Auth & Security for how it works if you're extending the web layer.

docs.title: If you need to lock this down today
docs.text:
Options, roughly in order of effort:

  1. Put the API behind a reverse proxy/gateway that enforces your own API-key or mTLS scheme.
  2. Restrict network access (VPC/firewall rules, VPN-only exposure).
  3. Wire up PSKAuthMiddleware yourself on the /api/v1 group in handler/entry.go if a shared-secret scheme is sufficient for your deployment.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text: POST /api/v1/claims/check is the main entry point for third-party integrations — check a claim (a question, a casual statement, a sentence pulled from a video transcript) against the knowledge base and get back a cited verdict.

docs.title: Request
docs.text:
{
  "text": "Does drinking cold water cause a cold?",
  "is_long": false
}
  • text (required) — the claim/message to check. Can be a direct question or an arbitrary sentence.
  • is_long (optional, default false) — controls the verbosity of formatted_message only: false gives a brief paraphrased explainer per sub-claim, true gives full reasoning plus citations. sub_claims/citations in the structured response are always fully populated either way.

docs.title: Response
docs.text:
Important: out-of-scope input (not health-related) is a normal 200 with in_scope: false — not an error. This system only takes health-related inquiries.

{
  "data": {
    "in_scope": true,
    "overall_summary": "...",
    "formatted_message": "...",
    "sub_claims": [
      {
        "claim": "Cold water causes a cold",
        "verdict": "contradicted",
        "severity": "routine",
        "recommend_medical_consult": false,
        "reasoning": "...",
        "brief_reasoning": "...",
        "citations": [
          {
            "index": 0,
            "source": "chunk",
            "document_id": "...",
            "chunk_id": "...",
            "text": "..."
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

When in_scope is false, refusal_reason explains why and every other field (overall_summary, formatted_message, sub_claims) is empty.

docs.title: Verdict values
docs.text: supported, contradicted, partially_supported, mixed, insufficient_evidence — the last one means the knowledge base had nothing relevant to check the claim against, not that the claim itself is right or wrong.

docs.title: Severity values
docs.text: routine, serious, emergency — combined with recommend_medical_consult, this signals when a sub-claim's subject matter warrants pointing the user at a real doctor rather than just an information lookup.

docs.title: Citations
docs.text: Each citation is either a document chunk or an extracted fact (atomic knowledge). index matches the inline [N] markers in reasoning. Combine document_id + chunk_id to deep-link into the evidence viewer: /evidence?document_id=...&chunk_id=... on the web UI.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: 400 for a malformed body, 422 if text is missing, 500 otherwise — see Errors.

docs.title: Documents
docs.text:
CRUD for documents in the knowledge base. Creating a document is what kicks off the async ingestion pipeline (parsing, chunking, embedding, knowledge extraction) — see Background Jobs for what happens after a 201.

Upload the file first via Media to get a file_key, then create the document record.

docs.title: Create — POST /api/v1/documents
docs.text:
Request body (dto.CreateDocumentDTO):

{
  "sha256": "…",
  "file_key": "documents/report.pdf",
  "title": "WHO Guidance on X",
  "filename": "report.pdf",
  "filetype": "application/pdf",
  "filesize": 483920,
  "page_count": 12,
  "publisher_name": "WHO",
  "publication_year": 2024,
  "language": "en"
}
  • language must be "en" or "fr" — it's required, not auto-detected.
  • file_key must be a key already uploaded via the media-upload flow.

Returns 201 with the created model.Document on success. 400 for a malformed body, 422 for a validation failure (missing/invalid fields), 500 otherwise.

docs.title: List — GET /api/v1/documents
docs.text:
Query params: page (default 1), per_page (default 20, max 100) — see Rate Limits for the pagination cap.

Returns 200 with a dto.PaginationResults[model.Document]:

{
  "data": {
    "page": 1,
    "per_page": 20,
    "total_items": 42,
    "items": [ { "id": "...", "title": "...", "...": "..." } ]
  }
}

docs.title: Get — GET /api/v1/documents/{id}
docs.text: Returns 200 with a single model.Document, or 404 if the ID doesn't exist.

docs.title: Update — PUT /api/v1/documents/{id}
docs.text:
Request body (dto.UpdateDocumentDTO) — only descriptive metadata is mutable; the underlying file, hash, and other physical attributes are immutable once ingested:

{ "title": "Updated title", "publisher_name": "WHO", "publication_year": 2024 }

Returns 200 with the updated model.Document. 404 if not found, 409 on a conflict, 422 on validation failure.

docs.title: Delete — DELETE /api/v1/documents/{id}
docs.text: Returns 204 No Content on success, 404 if not found.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: All endpoints share the standard error shape. Most document-specific failures surface as 404 (unknown ID) or 422 (validation — e.g. bad language value).

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Handlers return errors as model.APIError{Code, Internal, Public}. Code is the HTTP status to send, Public is the message that ends up in the response envelope's error field, and Internal is the (unexposed) underlying error used only for server-side logging.

{
  "request_id": "018f2e2b-...",
  "status": 404,
  "data": null,
  "error": "The requested resource could not be found"
}

docs.title: Status codes you'll see
docs.text:
Status When 400 Bad Request The request body couldn't be bound/parsed (invalid request body). 422 Unprocessable Entity The body parsed but failed validation (go-playground/validator rules on the DTO). 404 Not Found The requested resource doesn't exist. 409 Conflict The write conflicts with an existing resource. 403 Forbidden Insufficient permissions for the operation. 500 Internal Server Error An unexpected internal error, or any service-layer error not mapped to one of the above.

The 404/409/403/500 mapping comes from a fixed sentinel-error table in handler/errors.go (data.ErrNotFound, data.ErrConflict, data.ErrForbidden, data.ErrInternal) — anything else falls back to a generic 500 rather than leaking internal error details.

There is no separate machine-readable error code/taxonomy beyond the HTTP status — build client-side error handling around status (and, for validation failures, expect to re-check your request against the endpoint's documented fields).

docs.title: Media
docs.text: Two endpoints handle object storage (S3/MinIO, depending on STORAGE_PROVIDER) indirectly — the API never proxies file bytes itself, it only issues presigned URLs the client uploads/downloads with directly.

docs.title: Upload flow
docs.text:
1. GET /api/v1/media/upload — request a presigned POST policy before uploading a file.
Query param Required Notes intent yes document or document_image — determines the storage prefix (documents/, document_images/). filename yes The filename you intend to upload. content_type yes MIME type of the file.

Response (200): 

{
  "data": {
    "url": "https://s3.example.com/bucket",
    "prefix": "documents/",
    "formFields": { "key": "documents/report.pdf", "policy": "...", "...": "..." }
  }
}

POST the actual file directly to url as multipart/form-data, including every key in formFields plus a file field with the file content. The resulting object key is prefix + filename (e.g. documents/report.pdf) — that's the value to use as file_key when creating a document (see Documents).

Errors: 404/409 if the intent/filename combination can't be prepared, 422 for an invalid intent or malformed filename.

  1. GET /api/v1/media/presigned-url — get a temporary signed GET URL for an existing object.
Query param Required Notes s3_key yes Full object key, e.g. documents/report.pdf. ttl no Seconds until expiry. Default 900 (15 min), max 86400 (24h).

Response (200): 

{ "data": { "presigned_url": "https://s3.example.com/bucket/documents/report.pdf?...", "ttl": 900 } }

Errors: 400 for an invalid S3 key, 422 for a validation failure, 500 on an internal error.

docs.title: OpenAPI Spec
docs.text: A machine-readable Swagger 2.0 spec is generated from annotations on the handler functions (handler/*.go, e.g. the @Summary/@Param/@Success comments above each handler) using swag.

docs.title: Where it lives
docs.text:
• swagger/swagger.yaml
  • swagger/swagger.json
  • swagger/docs.go — the same spec embedded as a Go package (used if you wire up swaggo/echo-swagger to serve interactive docs from a running instance; not currently mounted).

It covers the three resource groups documented here: Documents, Media, and Claims.

docs.title: Viewing it
docs.text: The easiest way to explore it interactively today: paste the contents of swagger.yaml or swagger.json into editor.swagger.io, which renders a browsable, "try it out"-capable UI without needing a local server.

docs.title: Regenerating it
docs.text:
The spec is generated, not hand-written — never edit swagger/* directly. Regenerate it with:

go tool swag init -q --output ./swagger --generalInfo ./core/app.go

This is now wired into make check, so a stale spec (annotations edited without regenerating) will show up as a diff in swagger/ during review rather than silently drifting from the actual handlers.

docs.title: API Overview
docs.text: Wobsongo exposes a versioned REST API under /api/v1, mounted alongside the web UI on the same Echo instance (e.Group("/api") in core/app.go). It's the surface to use once the bundled web UI's forms aren't enough — e.g. ingesting documents programmatically, or checking a claim from a bot or another service.

docs.title: Base path
docs.text: https://<your-deployment-host>/api/v1

docs.title: Middleware
docs.text:
Every /api/v1/* route currently gets only the global middleware stack applied to the whole app:

  • panic recovery
  • a request ID (returned as the X-Request-ID response header)
  • CORS (allowed origins configured via CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS)
  • request logging

No authentication or rate limiting is applied at this layer today — see Authentication and Rate Limits for the specifics before you rely on either.

docs.title: Response envelope
docs.text:
Every handler returns the same JSON shape:

{
  "request_id": "018f2e2b-...",
  "status": 200,
  "data": { "...": "..." },
  "error": ""
}
  • request_id — echoes the X-Request-ID header, useful for correlating a support request with server logs.
  • status — the HTTP status code, duplicated in the body.
  • data — present on success, omitted on error.
  • error — a short public-safe message, present only on error.

See Errors for the full set of status codes and messages.

docs.title: Resources
docs.text: Resource Docs Documents (ingest, list, update, delete) Documents Media (presigned upload/download URLs) Media Claim checking Claims

docs.title: Machine-readable spec
docs.text: An OpenAPI (Swagger 2.0) spec is generated from the handler annotations — see OpenAPI Spec.

docs.title: Rate Limits
docs.text:
There is no rate limiting enforced on /api/v1/* today. (The web UI's /login endpoint has its own IP-based rate limiter, but that's a separate concern from the REST API.)

The only bound you'll run into is pagination: list endpoints accept page and per_page query parameters (dto.PaginationDTO), defaulting to 20 items per page with a hard cap of 100 per page — requesting more than 100 silently clamps to 100 rather than erroring.

If you're integrating a bot or automated pipeline against this API, be a good citizen and throttle client-side — a future release may add server-side limits without notice.

docs.title: Auth & Security
docs.text: Two independent auth schemes exist in this codebase, scoped to different route groups. They don't share code and aren't interchangeable.

docs.title: Web UI: JWT-in-cookie + CSRF
docs.text:
Applies to every route mounted via webhandler.RegisterWebRoutes (dashboard, documents, chunks, knowledge, retrieval, check, evidence).

  • auth.Auth (auth/auth.go) issues an access/refresh JWT pair (HS256, APP_JWT_SECRET, APP_JWT_EXPIRY_HOURS) on login/registration. Claims carry user_id, name, email, role.
  • handler.JWTFromCookieMiddleware pulls the token out of a named cookie; handler.JWTParserMiddleware validates it and, on success, attaches the claims to the request context via handler.ClaimsFromContext. An invalid/missing token is not an error at this stage — it just leaves the request unauthenticated.
  • webhandler.RequireAuthMiddleware is what actually enforces auth — it redirects to /login if ClaimsFromContext returns nil. It's applied to the protected route group in webhandler/entry.go.
  • webhandler.RequireRoleMiddleware(minimum) exists for role-gating but isn't applied to any route yet — reserved for future admin-only pages.
  • CSRF protection (middleware.CSRFWithConfig, form-field lookup _csrf) wraps the whole web route group in core/app.go.
  • Passwords are hashed with bcrypt (cost 12 in production, auth.WithMinCost() for tests/seed scripts) via auth/password.go.
  • /login has its own IP-based rate limiter (5 req/min, burst 2) — see webhandler/ratelimit.go.

docs.title: REST API: none today
docs.text:
/api/v1/* has no authentication applied — see API Authentication for the full picture. Two pieces of evidence this was planned but never finished:

  • A comment in handler/web_middleware.go says the API group "uses JWTFromHeaderMiddleware instead, if/when it needs auth" — that function doesn't exist anywhere in the codebase. It's an aspirational reference, not a real code path.
  • handler.PSKAuthMiddleware (pre-shared-key checker) exists and is fully implemented, but isn't attached to any route.

If you're adding API authentication, these are the two most-referenced starting points in the existing code — but treat both as unfinished scaffolding, not working features.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text: config.Config marks every credential field json:"-" (JWT secret, DB URI, S3/VLM/embedding/extraction/translation/claim-check API keys) so Config can be logged/inspected without leaking them. Never add a new secret field without the same tag.

docs.title: Background Jobs
docs.text:
Wobsongo uses River (Postgres-backed job queue) for everything that shouldn't block an HTTP response — document ingestion is entirely asynchronous after the initial POST /api/v1/documents call.

Job payloads/kinds are defined in queue/ (document.go, claim_check.go); the workers that process them live in worker/, and call only into service/ — never into repo/ or db/ directly (same layering rule as everything else, see Architecture).

docs.title: Document ingestion pipeline
docs.text:
POST /api/v1/documents
        │
        ▼
ParseDocumentWorker            fetches raw Docling output for the file, stores it in
                                object storage, enqueues the next job. Deliberately
                                does nothing else — Docling responses can be huge and
                                re-fetching from a rate-limited external service on
                                every retry would be wasteful.
        │
        ▼
ProcessParsedDocumentWorker    turns the stored raw output into DocumentChunk rows.
                                Never calls Docling itself, so it can retry freely.
                                Fans out to:
        │
        ├──▶ CaptionImageChunksWorker   generates captions for picture/chart chunks
        │        │                     (its own job so a slow/rate-limited VLM call
        │        │                     never fails or retries chunk storage itself).
        │        └──▶ re-enqueues EmbedChunks / ExtractKnowledge / TranslateChunks
        │             for the now-captioned (now text-bearing) chunks.
        │
        ├──▶ EmbedChunksWorker          computes + stores embeddings for text-bearing,
        │                               not-yet-embedded chunks (batched).
        │
        ├──▶ ExtractKnowledgeWorker     extracts atomic knowledge facts (subject-
        │        │                     predicate-object + truth tier) from text-bearing
        │        │                     chunks. Self-requeues to continue past its own
        │        │                     per-run batch limit on large documents.
        │        └──▶ enqueues EmbedKnowledgeWorker for the newly extracted facts.
        │
        └──▶ TranslateChunksWorker      translates text-bearing chunks into the other
                                        supported language, so bilingual full-text
                                        search finds them regardless of query language.

Each stage is its own job — not inlined into its predecessor — specifically so a slow, costly, or rate-limited external call (VLM captioning, embedding, extraction, translation) can fail/retry independently without re-doing already-completed work like chunk storage.

docs.title: Claim checking
docs.text: ClaimCheckWorker runs the full analyze → retrieve → judge pipeline for a piece of text (queue.ClaimCheckJob). Note: this is the async/queued path, distinct from the synchronous POST /api/v1/claims/check HTTP endpoint, which calls the same service layer directly and returns the verdict in the response. For async callback support (e.g. bot notifications after a queued check completes), the worker's own docs point at wrapping ClaimService directly rather than extending this worker.

docs.title: Concurrency tuning
docs.text: ExtractKnowledgeWorker/TranslateChunksWorker bound how many chunks they process concurrently via EXTRACTION_CONCURRENCY/TRANSLATION_CONCURRENCY (default 5 each) — tune based on your LLM backend's actual rate-limit tolerance, no code change needed.

docs.title: Database
docs.text: PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension for embedding similarity search.

docs.title: Migrations
docs.text:
sql/migrations/ holds paired up/down golang-migrate files, applied in order:

  1. init_schema — base schema.
  2. create_documents_table
  3. create_document_chunks_table
  4. add_document_chunk_embeddings
  5. create_atomic_knowledge_table
  6. add_atomic_knowledge_embeddings
  7. change_embedding_dimension_to_1024 — the reference pattern for changing embedding dimensions (see External Integrations).
  8. add_search_infra
  9. add_atomic_knowledge_category
  10. add_bilingual_search — adds the text_fts_en/text_fts_fr generated full-text-search columns and translated-text columns backing bilingual retrieval.
  11. add_user_auth_fields
  12. add_document_chunk_page_index
make migrateup     # apply all pending migrations
make migratedown   # roll back one

docs.title: sqlc
docs.text:
db/ is entirely generated from sql/queries/*.sql against the schema in sql/migrations/ — never hand-edit anything in db/. Config lives in sqlc.yaml.

go tool sqlc diff       # check for drift between queries/schema and generated code (part of `make check`)
go tool sqlc generate   # regenerate db/

Notable overrides in sqlc.yaml: uuid/timestamptz map to uuid.UUID/time.Time, and both embedding columns are forced to the pointer form of pgvector.Vector — the non-pointer form panics on scanning a NULL embedding (a chunk/fact that hasn't been embedded yet), verified empirically; the pointer form round-trips nil/NULL correctly via pgx's generic nil-pointer handling.

docs.title: Language / bilingual search
docs.text: Language (English/French) is stored as a plain integer, matching the existing TruthTier/FactCategory convention rather than a native Postgres enum. It's set explicitly at document ingestion — never auto-detected — and copied down onto document_chunks/atomic_knowledge rows at insert/extraction time (needed directly on each row since Postgres generated columns can't reference another table for the full-text search columns). TranslateChunksWorker/extraction populate a *_translated column per row so full-text search matches regardless of which language the search query is in.

docs.title: Adding a query
docs.text:
1. Write the SQL in sql/queries/<table>.sql following existing sqlc annotation conventions in that file.
  2. go tool sqlc generate (or sqlc diff to check first) to regenerate db/.
  3. Add the corresponding method to the relevant interface in data/, implement it in repo/ (one SQL statement per method — see Patterns & Conventions), and regenerate its mock via make gen.

docs.title: Makefile
docs.text: Command What it does make check go mod tidy → build → swag init (regen OpenAPI spec) → golangci-lint run → sqlc diff. Run before every PR. make fmt go fmt + golangci-lint fmt. make gen go generate ./... — regenerates mockrepo/ mocks (via moq, triggered by //go:generate directives) and anything else generate-driven. Does not regenerate sqlc or swagger — those are separate steps (sqlc diff/sqlc generate, swag init). make dev Runs the server with air hot-reload. make db Opens a psql shell to the local dev database. make dbup / dbstop / dbdown / dball Start / stop / remove / fully reset the local Postgres (via compose.yml). make migrateup / migratedown Run/rollback migrations. make reset Reset with seed data. make admin Create a local superadmin user (admin.com / LocalDev123). make dbtestup / dbtestdown Start/stop the isolated test database (test-compose.yaml) — required before make test. make test / test-unit / test-integration / testrace See Testing.

docs.title: Taskfile (frontend asset pipeline)
docs.text: Task What it does task setup-static One-time: copy JS assets, compile initial CSS. Run before first build if you haven't already. task dev Tailwind watch + templ generate --watch (which itself runs the server via go run, restarting on .go/.templ changes), proxied on :7331. task tailwind Tailwind CSS watch only. task templ templ generate --watch only, proxied on :7331 → :8000. task build Production build: compile CSS, generate templ, build the binary with embedded assets.

docs.title: Codegen tools
docs.text:
• sqlc — generates db/ from sql/queries/ + sql/migrations/. Run go tool sqlc diff to check for drift, go tool sqlc generate to regenerate. See Database.
  • moq — generates mocks in mockrepo/ from interfaces in data/, triggered by //go:generate directives on the interface source files. Run via make gen.
  • swag — generates the OpenAPI spec in swagger/ from handler annotations. Run via make check (wired into the check target) or standalone: go tool swag init -q --output ./swagger --generalInfo ./core/app.go. See OpenAPI Spec.
  • templ — generates _templ.go files from .templ templates in view/.

docs.title: Linting
docs.text: golangci-lint config lives in .golangci.json. Run via make check or golangci-lint run ./... directly inside devbox shell.

docs.title: ADRs
docs.text: Architecture Decision Records live as plain markdown in docs/adr/ and are linked directly into the mkdocs nav (see Architecture). devbox.json also defines adr/adr:preview/adr:build scripts wrapping log4brains, but log4brains has no config file in this repo and isn't currently wired up — those scripts won't work out of the box. Don't rely on them; write and link ADRs as plain markdown until/unless log4brains is properly configured.

docs.title: Worked example: adding a new embedding provider
docs.text:
Wobsongo already supports two embedding wire shapes behind one interface — see External Integrations for the existing openai/bge pattern. This walks through adding a third, e.g. a hypothetical cohere shape.

1. Everything hangs off one interface — data.Embedder (data/vector.go):

type Embedder interface {
    Embed(ctx context.Context, texts []string) ([][]float32, error)
}

Any type satisfying this can be swapped in without touching service/ or worker/ at all — they only ever call Embed.

2. Implement the client in external/cohere_client.go, following the existing EmbeddingClient/BGEClient shape:

package external

type CohereClient struct {
    baseURL, apiKey string
    httpClient      *http.Client
}

var _ data.Embedder = (*CohereClient)(nil)

func NewCohereClient(baseURL, apiKey string) *CohereClient { /* ... */ }

func (c *CohereClient) Embed(ctx context.Context, texts []string) ([][]float32, error) {
    // build the request in Cohere's wire shape, POST, parse, return vectors
    // in the same order as texts — re-sort by a response index field if the
    // API doesn't guarantee ordering (EmbeddingClient does this; BGEClient
    // doesn't need to because its API guarantees input order).
}

3. Add the provider constant in config/config.go:

const (
    EmbeddingProviderOpenAI = "openai"
    EmbeddingProviderBGE    = "bge"
    EmbeddingProviderCohere = "cohere" // new
)

Update IsEmbeddingOK's validation to accept it, and NewEmbeddingConfig if the new provider needs config fields beyond the existing BaseURL/Model/APIKey.

4. Wire the constructor in cmd/server.go's newEmbeddingClient:

func newEmbeddingClient(cfg *config.EmbeddingConfig) data.Embedder {
    switch cfg.Provider {
    case config.EmbeddingProviderBGE:
        return external.NewBGEClient(cfg.BaseURL, cfg.APIKey)
    case config.EmbeddingProviderCohere:
        return external.NewCohereClient(cfg.BaseURL, cfg.APIKey)
    default:
        return external.NewEmbeddingClient(cfg.BaseURL, cfg.Model, cfg.APIKey)
    }
}

5. Document the new env value in .env.example's EMBEDDING_PROVIDER comment block.

6. Test it the same way external/embedding_client_test.go does — spin up an httptest.Server that returns a fixed response in the new shape, assert Embed parses it correctly (including any index re-sorting), and assert the request body/auth header match what the real API expects.

No changes needed anywhere in service/, worker/, or handler/ — that's the point of depending on the data.Embedder interface rather than a concrete client type.

docs.title: The general pattern for any new feature
docs.text:
The embedding-provider example above is a case of swapping an implementation behind an existing interface. Adding a genuinely new capability (a new resource, a new verification module, a new storage backend) follows the fuller top-down checklist in Patterns & Conventions:

model/ → sql/queries/ (+ make gen) → data/ (interface) → repo/ (implementation)
       → mockrepo/ (+ make gen) → service/ → handler/ (or webhandler/)

Work through it in that order — each layer's interface should exist before you implement the layer below it, so the mock (and therefore the test for the layer above) is available as soon as you need it.

docs.title: External Integrations
docs.text:
All LLM/embedding/parsing backends are pluggable HTTP clients in external/, configured entirely through environment variables (config/config.go). Every one of them talks to a generic OpenAI-compatible (or documented alternative) wire shape, so they work unmodified against self-hosted vLLM/Ollama/text-embeddings-inference or a hosted provider using that shape — no code change needed to swap backends, only env vars.

Client Purpose Config prefix Notes external/docling.go Parses ingested documents (PDF/etc.) into structured layout + text via Docling Serve. DOCLING_BASE_URL Not gated behind a validity check like the others — always expected to be configured. external/vlm_client.go Generates captions for picture/chart chunks. Vision chat-completions API. VLM_* Required for the server to start. external/embedding_client.go / external/bge_client.go Computes embeddings for chunks and atomic-knowledge facts. EMBEDDING_* Two wire shapes behind one data.Embedder interface — see below. Required for the server to start. external/extraction_client.go Extracts atomic knowledge (subject-predicate-object facts + truth tier) from chunk text. Text-only reasoning. EXTRACTION_* Required for the server to start. EXTRACTION_CONCURRENCY (default 5) bounds parallel chunk processing. external/translation_client.go Translates chunk/fact text into the deployment's other supported language. TRANSLATION_* Defaults to the same backend as extraction in practice, but independently configurable. TRANSLATION_CONCURRENCY (default 5). external/claim_analyzer_client.go Scope/decomposition analysis for POST /api/v1/claims/check — is this in scope, what are the sub-claims. CLAIM_CHECK_* external/judge_client.go Verdict judging for claim checking — given retrieved evidence, decide supported/contradicted/etc. CLAIM_CHECK_* Shares config with the claim analyzer.

docs.title: The embedding dual-shape pattern
docs.text:
data.Embedder is a single-method interface (Embed(ctx, texts) ([][]float32, error)), and two implementations satisfy it:

  • EmbeddingClient — the default. Speaks the standard POST {baseURL}/v1/embeddings shape with {"model", "input"}, used by OpenAI, Ollama, LiteLLM, vLLM, etc. Re-sorts the response by its index field rather than trusting ordering.
  • BGEClient — for self-hosted BGE deployments that expose a simpler POST {baseURL} endpoint with {"texts": [...]} and no index field.

EMBEDDING_PROVIDER (openai default, or bge) selects which one cmd/server.go's newEmbeddingClient constructs. This is the reference pattern for adding a new provider of your own.

docs.title: Embedding dimension
docs.text: Embedding columns (document_chunks.embedding, atomic_knowledge.embedding) are fixed at 1024 dimensions, sized for BGE-M3. Switching to a model with a different output dimension requires a migration — see sql/migrations/000007_change_embedding_dimension_to_1024.up.sql for the pattern — and clearing existing embeddings so they get recomputed.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Jetify Devbox — provides a reproducible toolchain (Go, Node/pnpm, Python, golangci-lint, go-migrate, Tailwind, make) via Nix, so you don't need any of these installed globally.
  • Docker (for local Postgres/MinIO via compose.yml).

docs.title: First-time setup
docs.text:
git clone git@github.com:kairosedubf/wobsongo.git
cd wobsongo
devbox shell        # drops you into the reproducible toolchain
go mod download
cp .env.example .env  # then fill in the required values below

docs.title: Required env vars to get the server running
docs.text:
Per .env.example, these are required for the server to start (not just for full functionality):

  • APP_DB_URI, APP_JWT_SECRET
  • VLM_BASE_URL / VLM_MODEL (image captioning)
  • EMBEDDING_BASE_URL / EMBEDDING_MODEL (chunk + knowledge embeddings)
  • EXTRACTION_BASE_URL / EXTRACTION_MODEL (atomic knowledge extraction)

These point at OpenAI-compatible chat-completions/embeddings endpoints — self-hosted (vLLM, Ollama, text-embeddings-inference) or a hosted provider. See External Integrations for the full picture, including the bge embedding shape as an alternative to the default OpenAI-compatible one.

docs.title: Database
docs.text:
make dbup        # start Postgres (+ pgvector) via compose.yml
make migrateup   # run migrations

docs.title: Running the server
docs.text:
Two alternatives — don't run both at once, they fight over port 8000:

  • make dev — air hot-reload, plain go run, manual browser refresh. Also the option that regenerates swagger docs on rebuild (see the check target).
  • task dev — full auto-reload flow: templ generate --watch + Tailwind watch, proxied through :7331 → :8000. Browse via http://localhost:7331 (not :8000) to get live reload on .go/.templ/CSS changes.

First time using task dev, run task setup-static once beforehand to copy JS assets and compile the initial CSS bundle.

docs.title: Quality checks before committing
docs.text:
make check    # go mod tidy, build, swag regen, golangci-lint, sqlc diff
make test     # requires make dbtestup first — see Testing

See Dev Tooling for the full command reference and Testing for the test database setup.

docs.title: Patterns & Conventions
docs.text: The one rule that governs everything else: the service layer is the single entry point for business logic. Handlers, workers, and CLI commands are all just callers of service/ — none of them touch repo/ or db/ directly. Full rationale in ADR 0001; this page is the condensed DO/DON'T version for day-to-day work.

docs.title: DO
docs.text:
• Put business logic in service/, transport logic in handler//webhandler/. A handler binds a DTO, validates it, calls exactly one service method, and writes the response. If you're writing an if on domain data inside a handler, it belongs in the service.
  • Own transaction boundaries in the service layer. When multiple SQL ops must succeed or fail together, call repo.WithTx(ctx, func(txRepo) error { ... }) and compose individual repo calls inside. When a write must be atomic with enqueuing a job, do both inside the same WithTx() via txRepo.Enqueue().
  • Keep each repo method to exactly one SQL statement. No repo method calls another repo method; no repo method opens its own transaction. This is what makes every repo method trivially mockable.
  • Depend on interfaces (data/), not concrete types. Services take data.XRepoer interfaces, never *repo.XRepo directly — that's what makes mockrepo/ substitution possible in tests.
  • Follow the checklist for new features, top-down: model (model/) → SQL query (sql/queries/, then make gen) → repo interface (data/) → repo implementation (repo/) → mock (make gen) → service (service/) → handler (handler/). See Extending for a full worked example.
  • Map errors at the repo boundary. Repos translate driver-level errors (pgx.ErrNoRows, etc.) into typed sentinels (data.ErrNotFound, data.ErrConflict, ...). Handlers translate those sentinels into HTTP status codes via mapDataErrorToHTTP — don't hand-roll a new error-to-status mapping per handler.
  • Tag every secret field json:"-" on config.Config and anything derived from it.

docs.title: DON'T
docs.text: Anti-pattern Why it's wrong A repo method calls pgx.BeginFunc/pool.Begin Transactions belong at the service layer, not hidden in data access. A repo method performs more than one SQL statement Breaks the "trivially mockable" property and obscures business logic in the data layer. A worker opens its own DB connection or imports repo/db directly Bypasses the service layer, breaks the "workers are just another caller of service" invariant. A CLI command (cmd/) calls db.Queries directly Same reasoning as workers — no direct DB access outside service//repo/. A service imports db directly Services depend on repo interfaces, not SQLC output — otherwise swapping persistence details requires touching business logic. Hand-editing anything under db/ It's entirely sqlc-generated from sql/queries/ — edits get silently overwritten on the next sqlc generate.

docs.title: Verifiable in review
docs.text:
Two questions catch most layering violations at PR time:

  • Does this repo method contain more than one query call?
  • Does this worker (or CLI command) import repo or db?

If either is "yes," the change likely needs restructuring before merge.

docs.title: Project Structure
docs.text: Wobsongo is a flat-layout Go module — packages live at the repo root, there is no internal/ prefix anywhere in the codebase. (Older versions of this doc and the ADR referenced internal/... paths from an earlier refactor; those have been corrected. If you see internal/ mentioned elsewhere — old comments, a stale Makefile target — treat it as a leftover, not the real layout.)

docs.title: Top-level packages
docs.text: Package Purpose cmd/ Cobra CLI commands — serve, migrations, createsuperadmin, evaluation/backfill utilities. main.go just calls cmd.Execute(). core/ App wiring: builds the Echo instance, mounts /api and the web route group, registers middleware. config/ Environment-variable driven Config struct and per-feature sub-configs (S3, email, VLM, embedding, extraction, translation, claim-check). handler/ REST API transport layer (/api/v1/*) — binds/validates DTOs, calls one service method, writes the response. No business logic. webhandler/ HTML web UI transport layer — same transport-only rule as handler/, but for templ-rendered pages and JWT-cookie auth. service/ All business logic. The only layer allowed to depend on data/ interfaces; owns transaction boundaries. repo/ Persistence layer implementing the interfaces declared in data/. One SQL statement per method, no nested transactions. data/ Go interfaces for every repo and external provider — the contracts services depend on, and what mockrepo/ implements for tests. db/ sqlc-generated code from sql/queries/. Never hand-edited. model/ Domain types shared across layers (documents, users, verdicts, API envelope types). dto/ Wire-format request/response structs for the API (validation tags, JSON tags, pagination helpers). queue/ River job/payload definitions and the JobEnqueuer interface. worker/ River job handlers — the document/knowledge processing pipeline. Call service methods only, never repos or db directly. external/ HTTP clients for external services: Docling (parsing), VLM (captioning), embeddings, extraction/judge/claim-analyzer LLMs, translation. auth/ JWT issuing/parsing and password hashing used by the web UI's session auth. view/ templ templates (and their generated _templ.go companions) for the web UI. ui/ Embedded static assets (compiled CSS/JS) served by the web app. validation/ Custom go-playground/validator rules and DTO validation registration. mockrepo/ moq-generated mocks of the data/ interfaces, used in service-layer unit tests. testhelpers/ Shared test setup (DB, Echo test harness, response assertions). sql/ migrations/ (golang-migrate) and queries/ (sqlc source). swagger/ Generated OpenAPI/Swagger 2.0 spec (swag) — see OpenAPI Spec.

docs.title: Request flow at a glance
docs.text:
HTTP request
  → handler/ (or webhandler/)   transport: bind, validate, call service
  → service/                    business logic, transaction boundaries
  → repo/  (via data/ interfaces)  one SQL op per call
  → db/                         sqlc-generated queries

Background work follows the same rule one level removed: worker/ picks a job off the River queue and calls into service/ exactly like a handler would — it never reaches into repo/ or db/ directly. See Architecture for the full layering rules and ADR 0001 for the rationale.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: 80% line coverage is required for changed packages on every PR (per CONTRIBUTING.md).

docs.title: Unit vs. integration
docs.text:
Tests are split via the -short flag:

make test-unit          # go test -short -v ./... — no database required
make test-integration   # requires a running test database — repo-layer tests

Repo-layer tests are integration tests by nature (they exercise real SQL against Postgres) and are skipped in -short mode.

docs.title: Running the full suite
docs.text:
make dbtestup     # spins up an isolated Postgres (test-compose.yaml), creates the
                   # test user/DB, pre-creates the pgvector extension, runs migrations
make test         # runs everything with coverage, writes coverdb.profile
make dbtestdown   # tear down the test database

make test sets APP_ENV=testing and friends inline — you don't need a separate .env for it. Coverage excludes view//components/ packages (generated templ code) via -coverpkg.

make testrace     # same test run, with -race

docs.title: Test helpers (testhelpers/)
docs.text:
• SetupTestDB(t) — connects to APP_DB_URI (fails the test immediately if unset), returns a pool + db.Queries. Used by repo integration tests.
  • WithTxRollback(t, pool, fn) — runs fn inside a transaction that's always rolled back afterward, so each test gets a clean, isolated view of the database without truncating tables between runs.
  • echo.go — Echo test-request/context helpers.
  • response.go / statuscode.go — response-body and status-code assertion helpers for handler tests.

docs.title: Mocks (mockrepo/)
docs.text: Service-layer unit tests mock the data/ interfaces via moq-generated mocks in mockrepo/ — regenerate with make gen after changing an interface. See Patterns & Conventions for how repo interfaces/mocks fit into the layering rules, and Extending for a worked example that includes writing a service test against a mock.

docs.title: Our Pledge
docs.text:
We as members, contributors, and leaders pledge to make participation in our community a harassment-free experience for everyone, regardless of age, body size, visible or invisible disability, ethnicity, sex characteristics, gender identity and expression, level of experience, education, socio-economic status, nationality, personal appearance, race, religion, or sexual identity and orientation.

We pledge to act and interact in ways that contribute to an open, welcoming, diverse, inclusive, and healthy community.

docs.title: Our Standards
docs.text:
Examples of behavior that contributes to a positive environment for our community include:

  • Demonstrating empathy and kindness toward other people
  • Being respectful of differing opinions, viewpoints, and experiences
  • Giving and gracefully accepting constructive feedback
  • Accepting responsibility and apologizing to those affected by our mistakes, and learning from the experience
  • Focusing on what is best not just for us as individuals, but for the global health community we serve

docs.title: Enforcement Responsibilities
docs.text: Community leaders are responsible for clarifying and enforcing our standards of acceptable behavior and will take appropriate and fair corrective action in response to any behavior that they deem inappropriate, threatening, offensive, or harmful.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: This Code of Conduct applies within all community spaces, and also applies when an individual is officially representing the community in public spaces. Examples of representing our community include using an official e-mail address, posting via an official social media account, or acting as an appointed representative at an online or offline event.

docs.title: Enforcement

docs.title: Contributing to Wobsongo
docs.text:
Thank you for your interest in contributing to Wobsongo Verify! We are an open-source project dedicated to building standard infrastructure for automated claim verification.

Whether you are fixing a bug, adding a new Vector DB connector, or improving our documentation, we welcome your help.

docs.title: 1. Fork and Clone
docs.text:
Fork this repository to your own GitHub account and clone it locally:

git clone [https://github.com/ImpactScope-organization/wobsongo.git](https://github.com/ImpactScope-organization/wobsongo)
cd wobsongo

docs.title: 2. Set Up Environment
docs.text:
We use devbox for reproducible development environments. Initialize the environment and install all dependencies (including Go tooling) via our Makefile:

# Start the devbox environment
devbox shell

# Install Go modules and required tools
make setup

# Start local database dependencies via Docker
make dbup

docs.title: 3. Quality Assurance
docs.text:
All PRs must include tests and maintain at least 80% line coverage.

# Run only unit tests (skips integration tests)
make test-unit

# Run integration tests (requires local test DB)
make test-integration

# Run all tests with coverage report
make test

Test conventions:

  • File names: *_test.go — place test files alongside the source module.
  • Mocking: Use interface-based mocking.
  • Test data: Use isolated fixtures in tests/data/ or generated mock data; never use real production data.

Linting & Formatting: Run before opening a PR — CI will reject on failures:

# Formats code and runs golangci-lint
make check

docs.title: Data Privacy & Safety Policy
docs.text:
CRITICAL: Do not commit any real user data, private health records, or proprietary knowledge base dumps to this repository.

  • Use Dummy Data: When writing tests or examples, use the dummy data provided in tests/data/.
  • No API Keys: Never hardcode OpenAI or Vector DB keys. Use environment variables (e.g., .env).

docs.title: Pull Request Process
docs.text:
• Clone/fork the repo. We recommend forking to your own GitHub account and cloning locally.
  • Take on an issue or start a new feature. If you want to work on an existing issue, comment on it to let others know you're working on it.
  • Create a new branch for your feature: git checkout -b feature/my-new-feature
  • Commit your changes using clear messages: git commit -m "feat(vector): add Qdrant support to Retriever"
  • Push to your branch: git push origin feature/my-new-feature
  • Open a Pull Request against the main branch.
  • Wait for a maintainer to review. We aim to review all PRs within 72 hours.
  • Make sure that all checks pass (tests, linting, coverage) in GitHub Actions.
  • Once you get an approval, one of the project maintainers will merge your PR.

docs.title: Reporting Bugs
docs.text:
If you find a bug, please open an issue on GitHub. Include:

  • A clear title and description.
  • Steps to reproduce the bug. A clone or a fork of the repo with reproduction steps is ideal.
  • The version of Go, Devbox, and dependencies you are using. (although we always recommend using the versions in devbox.lock).

docs.title: Security Vulnerabilities
docs.text:
If you discover a security vulnerability, please do NOT open a public issue. Email tahta@impactscope.com instead. We will work with you to patch it before disclosing it publicly.

By contributing to this project, you agree to abide by our Code of Conduct.

docs.title: 1. Vision
docs.text: To create a standardized, accessible, and transparent infrastructure for automated truth verification, empowering organizations globally to combat misinformation in their local contexts.

docs.title: 2. Governance
docs.text:
• Project Lead: ImpactScope team as KAIROS' technical partner (maintains core roadmap and release cycle).
  • Maintainers: ImpactScope team is responsible for reviewing Pull Requests and patching security vulnerabilities.
  • Community: Open to contributions from NGOs, researchers, and developers.

docs.title: 3. Sustainability Plan
docs.text: This project is the core engine of the commercial Wobsongo Platform. KAIROS is contractually committed to maintaining this open-source repository as part of its business operations, ensuring long-term updates and bug fixes.

docs.title: 4. Roadmap
docs.text:
• Q1 2026: Release generic interfaces for Vector DBs (Weaviate, Qdrant).
  • Q2 2026: Add support for local LLMs (Llama 3, Mistral) for offline usage.
  • Q3 2026: Release benchmark datasets for low-resource languages (Moore, Fula).
  • Q4 2026: Release a web-based demo platform for easy testing and deployment, stable v1.0.0 release.

docs.title: 5. DPG Standards Compliance
docs.text:
• Open Source: Apache 2.0 License.
  • Open Standards: Uses JSON for data interchange and standard SQL/Vector interfaces.
  • Do No Harm: The system includes safety guardrails in the default prompts to prevent the generation of harmful content.
  • Licensing Strategy: Permissive (Apache 2.0). Reasoning: We chose a permissive license to maximize adoption by governments, NGOs, and private sector partners. This allows the "Wobsongo Verify" engine to be integrated into diverse software ecosystems (both open and proprietary) without legal friction, ensuring the widest possible impact for SDG 3.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text: The vocabulary used throughout this documentation, in the order you'll encounter it.

docs.title: Document
docs.text: The source file you ingest — a PDF, Word doc, or similar. Every document is tagged with a required language (en or fr) at ingestion time — this is never auto-detected, since a wrong guess would silently mis-tag content in a bilingual deployment.

docs.title: Chunk
docs.text: A parsed, page-positioned piece of a document — roughly a paragraph, table, or image, classified by layout type (title, section header, paragraph, list item, table, picture, chart, ...). Chunks are the unit that gets embedded and searched; a document is broken into many chunks during ingestion.

docs.title: Atomic knowledge
docs.text:
A single extracted fact — a subject/predicate/object triple — derived from a chunk's text. One chunk can yield multiple atomic-knowledge entries. Each is tagged with:

  • a truth tier: axiomatic, temporal, probabilistic, subjective, unknown, or invalid — how epistemically reliable the statement is.
  • a category: clinical (substantive health content) vs. metadata (administrative/bibliographic content about the document itself, e.g. authorship).

docs.title: Claim check
docs.text:
The core feature: submit a claim, question, or a sentence pulled from a transcript, and get back a verdict for each sub-claim it decomposes into:

  • Verdict — supported, contradicted, partially_supported, mixed, or insufficient_evidence.
  • Severity — routine, serious, or emergency — signals whether the subject matter warrants recommending a real medical consult.

insufficient_evidence means the knowledge base had nothing relevant to check the claim against — it does not mean the claim itself is right or wrong. This is the single most common point of confusion for a new integrator; keep it in mind when interpreting results (see also Claims).

docs.title: Citation
docs.text: A specific chunk or atomic-knowledge fact that a verdict is based on. Citations link back to the evidence viewer, which shows the exact passage in its original document context.

docs.title: Retrieval
docs.text: The hybrid search (full-text + vector similarity, across both chunks and atomic-knowledge facts, bilingual) that claim-checking runs internally to find relevant evidence. It's also exposed directly as its own search/inspection tool in the web UI — useful for understanding why a verdict came out the way it did, or for exploring the knowledge base independent of claim-checking.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Wobsongo is an open-source backend for automated claim verification. Feed it documents — official health guidance, fact sheets, guidelines — and it builds a structured, searchable knowledge base out of them; submit a claim or question, and it checks that claim against the knowledge base and returns a cited, per-sub-claim verdict rather than a single yes/no.

Under the hood: a REST API (Go/Echo) fronts an async ingestion pipeline (parsing → chunking → embedding → knowledge extraction, via a Postgres-backed job queue) and a hybrid retrieval layer (full-text + vector search, bilingual English/French) that both the claim-checking feature and a standalone search tool draw on.

docs.title: How you'd use it
docs.text:
• Web UI — hands-on document management and claim-checking without writing any code. See Web UI.
  • REST API — integrate ingestion and claim-checking into your own application or bot. See API Reference — this is the surface to use once the web UI's forms aren't enough for your workflow.
  • CLI — bulk operations, admin tasks, and evaluation tooling (cmd/) for operators running their own deployment. See Developer Guide.

docs.title: Why this exists
docs.text:
Wobsongo contributes to:

  • SDG 3 (Good Health & Well-being) — infrastructure to combat health misinformation with cited, sourced answers instead of unverified claims.
  • SDG 16 (Peace, Justice, Strong Institutions) — transparent fact-checking of public information, where every verdict traces back to a specific document and passage.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• New to the domain vocabulary (chunks, atomic knowledge, verdicts)? Start with Concepts.
  • Want to run it and try it yourself? Go to Quickstart.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: The fastest path to a working instance. This mirrors Local Setup but framed for trying the product out rather than contributing code — see that page for the full contributor-oriented detail.

docs.title: 1. Get the toolchain and database running
docs.text:
git clone git@github.com:kairosedubf/wobsongo.git
cd wobsongo
devbox shell
go mod download
make dbup
make migrateup

docs.title: 2. Configure external services
docs.text: Wobsongo needs a VLM (image captioning), an embedding endpoint, and a text-extraction endpoint configured to fully process documents and answer claim checks — these are required for the server to start, not optional extras. See External Integrations for what to point them at (self-hosted vLLM/Ollama, or a hosted provider). Without these configured, the server won't come up at all.

docs.title: 3. Start the server
docs.text: make dev

docs.title: 4. Try it
docs.text:
Via the web UI — visit http://localhost:8000/register, create an account, log in, and upload a document. Once it's finished processing (parsing → chunking → embedding → knowledge extraction runs asynchronously), use Check to ask a claim against it. See Web UI for a full walkthrough of every screen.

Via the API — once you have a document ingested (via the web UI or POST /api/v1/documents), check a claim directly:

curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/v1/claims/check \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"text": "Does drinking cold water cause a cold?"}'

See API Reference for the full endpoint surface.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Unfamiliar with the domain vocabulary used above (chunks, atomic knowledge, verdicts)? Read Concepts first.
  • Building against the API rather than clicking through the UI? Jump straight to API Reference.

docs.title: Use Cases
docs.text: Concrete scenarios for deploying Wobsongo, grounded in capabilities documented elsewhere in this site.

docs.title: Health guidance chatbot for an NGO or ministry of health
docs.text: Ingest a set of official guidance documents (WHO/national health authority publications, vaccination fact sheets, outbreak advisories) and expose claim-checking behind a messaging-bot integration — the codebase itself anticipates this pattern: ClaimCheckWorker's own documentation notes that async callback support "e.g. WhatsApp bot notifications" is meant to be built by wrapping the claim-checking service directly. Users ask questions in natural language; every answer traces back to a cited passage in an authoritative source document rather than an unsourced model response. See Claims for the response shape a bot integration would consume.

docs.title: Research tool for a fact-checking newsroom
docs.text: Ingest a body of source documents (scientific literature, official statements, prior fact-checks) and use Retrieval as a research aid — journalists can search the knowledge base directly to find and verify supporting or contradicting evidence for a claim under investigation, independent of running a full claim check. The evidence viewer lets them pull up the exact page a piece of evidence came from for citation in their own reporting.

docs.title: Severity-aware public-health triage
docs.text: Because every claim-check verdict carries both a truth verdict and a severity (routine/serious/emergency) plus a recommend_medical_consult flag (see Concepts), a hotline or self-service tool built on the API can route responses differently by risk: routine misinformation gets an informational correction, while a claim whose subject matter is flagged serious or emergency-severity can be steered toward recommending professional medical attention rather than treating the automated answer as sufficient on its own.

docs.title: Multilingual public information portal
docs.text: Bilingual (English/French) ingestion and search means a single knowledge base serves both languages without maintaining separate content — a document tagged in one language is discoverable via full-text search in the other automatically (see Database). Useful for organizations serving mixed-language populations without duplicating their document-ingestion effort per language.

docs.title: Web UI
docs.text: A walkthrough of every screen, in the order they appear in the sidebar. All screens except Evidence require logging in (RequireAuthMiddleware) — none are currently gated further by role, even though the code has an unused RequireRoleMiddleware reserved for future admin-only pages.

docs.title: Dashboard
docs.text:
(Screenshot: dashboard — to be added)

Currently a minimal placeholder: a welcome message with your name and a note that there's nothing here yet. It's not a metrics/summary dashboard today — don't expect stats or activity feeds.

docs.title: Documents
docs.text:
(Screenshot: documents list — to be added)

A paginated table (20/page) of every ingested document: Title (falls back to filename if untitled), Type (MIME type), Size, Language, Status (Ingested once processing has completed, Pending otherwise), and Uploaded date, with Edit/Delete actions per row.

(Screenshot: new document form — to be added)

Uploading a new document here is a plain, synchronous form submission — you pick a file (PDF, Word, RTF, HTML, Markdown, or an image; 50MB max) and fill in Title, Publisher, Publication year, and required Language (English/French), then submit. This uploads the file directly as part of the form POST and hashes it server-side.

This differs from the REST API's upload flow

The API's document-creation endpoint expects you to already have a file_key from a separate presigned-URL upload step (see Media) — the web UI does not use that two-step flow. If you're scripting ingestion, follow the API docs, not this page's upload mechanic.

Editing a document only lets you change Title, Publisher, and Publication year — the file itself and its Language are immutable once uploaded.

docs.title: Chunks
docs.text:
(Screenshot: chunks view — to be added)

Pick a document from the dropdown to see its chunks, one PDF page at a time (with a page-jump selector for documents with multiple pages). Each row shows the chunk's sequence number, layout type (paragraph, table, picture, etc.), language, and a truncated text preview. Selecting or hovering a row highlights that chunk's exact location on the page in an embedded PDF viewer alongside the table.

docs.title: Knowledge
docs.text:
(Screenshot: knowledge view — to be added)

Same document-picker pattern as Chunks. Shows the atomic-knowledge facts extracted from that document's chunks: Subject, Predicate, Object, Truth Tier, Category, and when it was extracted. This view is read-only — there's currently no way to flag or invalidate a fact from the UI (the underlying data model supports marking a fact invalid, but nothing surfaces that control here yet).

docs.title: Retrieval
docs.text:
(Screenshot: retrieval search — to be added)

A search box that runs the same hybrid retrieval claim-checking uses internally, directly exposed as a standalone tool — useful for exploring what's in the knowledge base or understanding why a claim check turned out the way it did. Each result is tagged as a chunk or a fact hit, shown alongside its source document, page (or truth tier, for a fact hit), and a text preview; hovering a result shows its match in the same embedded PDF viewer used on the Chunks page.

docs.title: Check
docs.text:
(Screenshot: claim check form — to be added)

The claim-checking form: enter your claim or question, choose Short or Long detail level, and submit. The result mirrors the API's claim-check response exactly — an overall summary, then one card per sub-claim with its verdict, severity, and reasoning (brief or full, depending on the detail level you chose). In Long mode, each card also lists its citations, linking to the evidence viewer below. See Claims for what each verdict/severity value means.

docs.title: Evidence viewer
docs.text:
(Screenshot: evidence viewer — to be added)

A standalone page (no sidebar) reached by clicking a citation from the Check page — not something you navigate to directly. It shows the exact page of the source PDF with the cited chunk's location highlighted, so you can verify a claim's evidence in its original context. PDF documents only.

docs.title: Login / Register
docs.text: Standard email/password authentication. Registration requires a password of at least 8 characters with at least two of: letters, digits, symbols.
